name: The Avery-MacLeod-McCarty Experiment
statement: By destroying each candidate molecule in turn, they showed the substance that carries heredity is DNA.
statementAccent: the substance that carries heredity is DNA
meaning: The Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment was a set of experiments performed by Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty at the Rockefeller Institute, published in 1944, which identified DNA as the chemical substance responsible for heredity, the first strong evidence that genes are made of DNA. Their work built directly on Frederick Griffith's 1928 discovery that a transforming principle from dead virulent pneumococcus bacteria could permanently and heritably convert harmless bacteria into the virulent form. Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty set out to determine the chemical nature of that transforming principle. They prepared purified extracts from the dead virulent bacteria and treated separate samples with enzymes that destroy specific classes of molecule: proteases to destroy proteins, ribonuclease to destroy RNA, and deoxyribonuclease to destroy DNA. They found that destroying the proteins or the RNA did not stop transformation, but destroying the DNA abolished it completely. This showed that DNA is the transforming principle, the molecule that carries the hereditary information. The finding was a landmark, though it met considerable skepticism at the time because many scientists believed the genetic material must be protein, and it was confirmed by the Hershey-Chase experiment in 1952.
mechanism: The experiment identified the hereditary molecule by a process of elimination, selectively destroying each candidate substance and seeing which loss abolished the transforming activity. Starting from heat-killed virulent smooth pneumococcus, the researchers purified an extract that retained the ability to transform harmless rough bacteria into the virulent smooth form, the transforming principle Griffith had discovered. They then took this active extract and treated separate portions with enzymes each specific to one type of biological molecule. Protein-digesting enzymes, proteases such as trypsin and chymotrypsin, destroyed the proteins in the extract, but the treated extract still transformed bacteria, ruling out protein. Ribonuclease, which destroys RNA, likewise left the transforming activity intact, ruling out RNA. But when they treated the extract with deoxyribonuclease, an enzyme that specifically breaks down DNA, the transforming activity was destroyed. Because only the destruction of DNA abolished the ability to transform, DNA had to be the transforming principle. They further supported this with chemical analyses showing the active substance had the properties of DNA. The logic was that the molecule whose destruction eliminates the hereditary effect must be the molecule carrying the hereditary information, and that molecule was DNA.

examples.text: Treating the extract with enzymes that destroy protein or RNA did not stop transformation, ruling those molecules out.
Treating the extract with deoxyribonuclease, which destroys DNA, abolished transformation, showing DNA is the transforming principle.
The work identified the chemical nature of the transforming principle Griffith had discovered in 1928 as DNA.

whyItMatters: The Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment is a landmark in the history of biology because it provided the first strong, direct evidence that DNA is the genetic material, the molecule that carries hereditary information. By showing that destroying the DNA in a bacterial extract, and only the DNA, abolished its ability to transmit a heritable trait, the experiment identified DNA as the transforming principle that Griffith had discovered but could not name, overturning the widespread assumption that genes must be made of protein. This was a foundational step in the birth of molecular biology, focusing attention on DNA as the central molecule of heredity and helping motivate the work that led to the double helix in 1953. The experiment is also a notable case study in how science handles unexpected results: because DNA was thought too chemically simple to carry the complexity of life, the finding met years of skepticism before being widely accepted, and Avery, despite the profound importance of the work, never received a Nobel Prize, a frequently cited omission.

working.text: prepare from dead virulent bacteria an extract that still transforms harmless bacteria into the virulent form.
treat separate samples with enzymes that destroy protein, RNA, or DNA, and test whether transformation survives.
find that only destroying the DNA abolishes transformation, showing DNA is the hereditary transforming principle.

limits: The Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment gave strong evidence that DNA is the genetic material, but it was not immediately accepted as conclusive, and its limits explain why. Because DNA was then thought to be a monotonous, chemically simple molecule of only four repeating units, many scientists doubted it could carry the complexity of heredity and suspected that a trace of protein contaminating the extract might be the real transforming agent, so the result met years of skepticism and was only widely accepted after the Hershey-Chase experiment in 1952 reinforced it. The work was carried out in a single bacterial system, pneumococcal transformation, so generalizing to all life required further evidence. Avery himself was characteristically cautious in his claims.
misreadings: The Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment was not instantly accepted as proving DNA is the genetic material; because DNA seemed too simple, many suspected protein contamination, and the finding met years of skepticism before Hershey-Chase reinforced it. It did not by itself prove the point for all life, since it worked in one bacterial system. And it identified the chemical nature of Griffith's transforming principle rather than discovering transformation itself, so treating the experiment as immediately convincing, as universally conclusive alone, or as the discovery of transformation, misreads the pivotal identification of DNA as the hereditary molecule.
origin: Experiments by Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty at the Rockefeller Institute, published in 1944, identifying DNA as the transforming principle and the first strong evidence that DNA is the genetic material.
